variants.verdict: This is a solid, faithful control. It keeps round 1's charm and fixes every panel flaw that was measured: figure weight, yellow contrast through the keyline, the roller as a cylinder, the sprayer clear of the torso, the hang-lines and the sun clash. The sun gag shows the art direction has a sense of humour. It is the safest baseline for the final style, and the figure, weapon and keyline rules should carry forward almost verbatim. Its weaknesses are expected for a control. The black keyline makes the paint chunky and less leaky than round 1. The drips are sparse and regular. The background gags are too faint to count as "maximalism" at gameplay scale, so the screenshot still reads as clean and minimal, a little sterile for a store capsule. Execution is about 8/10. As a final direction on its own it is about 6/10. Merge its figure, weapon and keyline rules with a variation that brings real background density and wetter, more irregular paint.

identity.reason: A faithful, clean control that fixes every round-1 flaw: figure weight, keylines, the roller cylinder, the sprayer placement and the grey sun gag. It is not maximal at all, though. At gameplay scale it reads as white space with pale doodles that vanish.

production.reason: A clean, faithful control. All the round-1 fixes land (7px figures, keylined paint, cylinder roller, grey sun gag, no hang-lines). But it is still mostly white space and its pale gags vanish at 480x270, so it does not answer the 'maximalism' the author asked for. Its rules carry forward, but its look does not.

player.reason: A clean, faithful control, and every round-1 flaw is fixed (figures, keyline, roller, sprayer, the sun gag). Its rules carry forward, but it reads as minimal, not maximal: the pale gags vanish at 480x270 and the scene is mostly white space.

variants.name: True Maximalism
variants.brief: Deliver the "maximalism" round 1 did not: a loud, dense, gleefully overloaded MS Paint canvas. Use full default-palette bucket fills that leak through gaps, WordArt-style rainbow text tags, stamped repeated clip shapes, overlapping doodles, a hand-drawn mouse-wobbly sky with multiple suns and a "hello" scrawled on it. Players and paint still have to read: use a value system (busy background desaturated or lighter, or kept behind a pale haze layer, with dark-outlined players and keylined paint). Take the risk; this exists to test how far loud can go.
variants.one_liner: A packed MS Paint canvas behind a pale haze. It has three suns (none yellow), a scrawled "hello!", WordArt tags, stamped clouds, hearts and stars, a bucket fill that leaked through a gap with an "oops", and a cat. The players and paint are die-cut stickers on top, so they still read at quarter-pane size.
variants.changed: The round-1 canvas was mostly white with quiet grey doodles. This one is a full Win7-Paint-palette world: a turquoise sky, a rainbow, purple and brown hills, a house, trees and a cat. Clip shapes are pasted over and over: the same cloud five times with the last paste still selected, plus rows of stars and hearts, and smiley and star stamps on every platform face. There are three suns (red with sunglasses, purple "sun 2", and a selected white "sun 3 (copy)"), a big mouse-drawn "hello!", WordArt "COLOUR WARS", "WOW!!", "SPLAT" and "PAINT!" with stepped extrusions, eraser bites, zigzags, spirals, airbrush graffiti, and a brown hill whose outline has a gap: its fill leaked into the inside of the rainbow, marked "oops". Readability comes from a three-tier value system. (1) The whole backdrop sits under a 38% white haze. (2) Structures are mid-dark palette blocks: grey floor and step, plus maroon, purple and teal platforms. Each has a light walkable lip and a 5px ink outline. (3) Owned things are stickers made with feMorphology. Paint gets a black keyline and a white halo. Players get their black lines, a white halo and a black rim. How this answers the panel: figures now have 6px limbs, a filled shirt, a bigger cap, a solid black brim and 5px eyes, and they read clearly at 480x270. Yellow paint is keylined and halo'd, and the sheet proves it on all four surfaces. No sun is yellow, and every team hue is kept out of the world; a joke says so ("rainbow (some colours are TAKEN by the teams)"). The maximalism is actually delivered this time. The sprayer is now a backpack tank with a team-colour gauge, a hose and a lance with a team nozzle, so nothing overlaps the torso. The roller is drawn as a tube: a rounded near end, a grey end cap with an axle, and a cranked wire into the near axle on a long angled handle. The hang-lines are gone. The deliberateness comes from repeated rules and labelled jokes ("do not move this cloud", "untitled - Paint", "CW woz here"). The sheet shows every pose over a hazed busy strip, a 3 pairs x 4 surfaces score grid, and an actual-size line-up of all six team colours over the busiest backdrop.
rules: Three value tiers, never mixed: the background is fully loud but always sits under a ~38% white haze. Structures are mid-dark Paint-palette blocks (grey #7F7F7F, maroon #880015, purple #A349A4, teal #008080) with a light walkable lip and a 5px ink outline. Anything a team owns is a sticker on top.

The sticker outline rules (square-kernel dilate, so they stay blocky). Paint is the colour, then a 2.5px black keyline, then a 5px white halo. Players and their gear are black pencil lines, then a 5px white halo, then a 7px black rim. Never apply either outline to anything in the world.

The team hues (blue, orange, pink, green, yellow) are TAKEN. The world uses only the rest of the Paint palette: red, maroon, purple, lavender, turquoise, teal, brown and greys. That holds for suns and rainbows too, and the scene makes it a joke.

Everything is made with a Paint tool. Pencil lines are aliased and mouse-wobbled. Fills come from the bucket and leave white pinholes, and a broken outline leaks its fill into the next region. The airbrush makes square specks. Stamps are identical pastes made with the same seed, and the last paste still shows its marching-ants selection.

Every joke is labelled with the Comic Sans text tool and stays in the background tier: oops, sun 2, sun 3 (copy), do not move this cloud, cat, untitled - Paint. WordArt gets a gradient face, a 4px ink stroke and a stepped grey extrusion. The background never has stick figures, box heads or flat team-colour regions that could be mistaken for a player or paint.

The figure is a box-head about 120 units tall: 6px limbs, a filled team shirt and cap crown, a solid black brim, two 5px dot eyes and a one-line mouth. Gear keeps its team region separate: the sprayer's tank gauge and nozzle, the roller's sleeve. The tank goes on the back, never over the torso.
Busy is allowed anywhere except the walkable tops. Stamp patterns on structures stay below the 8px lip, so the score surface is a clean band that paint sits on.
variants.self: The scene gives a real maximal overload and still passes at 480x270. Both players pop as white-haloed die-cuts, and the blue and orange paint bands read clearly on every surface. The sheet's 3x4 swatch grid shows that pink/green and blue/yellow hold up on grey, maroon, purple and teal. The yellow on teal and the blue on teal and purple are the weakest pairs, and they hold up only because of the halo. The sticker filter carries much of the load. Paint spray-ends and mist pick up chunky halos that read as spatter but are a little noisy. The haze makes the loud palette pastel-loud rather than fully saturated; at 0.38 it is about as low as it can go before the WordArt and suns start competing with the players. Weaker points: the "COLOUR WARS" arc barely curves. The bucket-leak joke needs its "oops" label to read. The upper sky (the clouds, "hello!" and the suns) is denser than the lower middle. The runtime cost of morphology outlines on paint would need checking, or it would have to be baked into the paint stamps. TAKEN team hues: the world uses only the non-team part of the Paint palette, including suns and rainbows, and a labelled joke says so. It is a cheap, enforceable rule that protects the read of paint.
The black keyline plus white halo on paint, which makes yellow and pink/green survive on every structure colour. The 3 pairs x 4 surfaces proof grid should become the standard acceptance sheet.
The figure upgrade: 6px limbs, a filled team shirt, a bigger cap with a solid black brim and 5px dot eyes. The actual-size line-up shows it still reads over the busiest backdrop.

Background density at the current level across every stage. In the 480x270 pane the upper sky (clouds, suns, hello, WordArt) is a wall of noise, and the blue sprayer player is the hardest thing in the frame to find. The bucket-leak 'oops' gag as it stands. It only reads because of its label and costs authored art per stage.
variants.verdict: This is the strongest systems thinking of the Paint.exe variations, and it is a bit too loud in execution. The value tiers, the TAKEN-hue rule, keylined and haloed paint, the tank-gauge sprayer, the tube roller and the beefed-up figure are all worth carrying straight into the final style, and the character sheet proves them (the swatch grid and the busy line-up are exemplary). The scene does deliver real maximalism and looks great as a capsule or trailer frame. As a gameplay frame at 480x270, though, the sky is overloaded. The 'hello!' scrawl, the red sun, the rainbow and the WordArt pull focus, and the blue sprayer player takes a beat to find. The halo outlines rescue paint contrast, but on airborne spray they get noisy. It also drifts somewhat from the author's spare round-1 Paint look toward a sticker-book collage. Making this kind of busy backdrop for every stage is expensive for a solo developer. Recommendation: adopt the rules and the gear and figure redesigns, cut the background loudness to roughly half (keep the jokes, labels and stamps, but lose the dark scrawls and the big WordArt), and keep full-loud for the title screen and store capsule.

identity.reason: The only variation that delivers literal maximalism, and it has the best capsule appeal. Its three-tier value system (hazed backdrop, mid-dark structure, outlined owned things) and the TAKEN-hue rule are essential takeaways. As a gameplay frame it is overloaded: the 'hello!' scrawl, the red sun and the WordArt pull focus, and the blue player is hard to find at 480x270. Keep it for the title screen, the capsule, and the edges of a busy stage.

production.reason: The best capsule and title frame, and the best systems doc (value tiers, TAKEN hues, a pairs-by-surfaces proof grid). As a gameplay pane it is overloaded: the 'hello!' scrawl, the red sun, the rainbow and the WordArt pull focus, the blue player is hard to find, the halos on spray are confetti, and building a backdrop like this for each stage is expensive. Keep it for the title screen and menus.

player.reason: The only one that actually delivers maximalism, and the best trailer or capsule frame by far. Its three-tier value system (hazed backdrop, mid-dark lipped structures, haloed sticker players and paint) is the key systems idea. At 480x270, though, the sky is a wall of noise: the dark 'hello!', the red sunglasses sun, the rainbow and the WordArt pull focus, and the blue sprayer player takes a beat to find. Cut the background loudness by roughly half for gameplay, and keep full-loud for the title screen and the capsule.

variants.name: Tool Props
variants.brief: The arena is built from Paint's own tools and canvas artefacts: platforms that are a giant pencil lying sideways, an eraser block, a selection rectangle with marching ants, a text-tool box with a blinking caret, the colour-palette swatch strip as a floor, a canvas resize handle as a step, the paint-bucket and spray-can icons as huge props, and "Untitled" faintly as a backdrop. Characters stay box-head Paint painters. No window chrome or menus: those are UI and come later. The world is made of tools.
variants.one_liner: A Paint canvas where the level is built from Paint's own tools. The floor is the colour-palette strip, the ramp is the sharpened end of a giant crimson pencil, and the floating platforms are an eraser, a selection with marching ants and a text box that literally says "platform|". Faint grey icons of the bucket, magnifier, brush and spray can hang behind a huge ghosted "Untitled".
variants.changed:
Round 1 was grey slabs hung on wires under doodled clouds. Here every structure is a recognisable Paint tool or canvas artefact. The floor is the palette strip in two rows of sunken swatch wells. The step on the left is a canvas resize handle with the diagonal resize cursor drawn on it. The ramp is the sharpened cone of a lying pencil (crimson facets, scalloped wood, graphite tip, then a ferrule and a lavender eraser cap). The floating platforms are a two-tone eraser block that leaves shavings, a text box holding "platform" with a blinking caret (SMIL), and a selection rectangle with animated marching ants and corner handles. Behind them, "Untitled" is typed huge in #E6E6E6. A bucket icon spills a fill that leaked through a gap, and there are a magnifier showing big pixels, a brush, a spray can with its airbrush cloud, and an unfinished curve-tool squiggle with its control points. An eyedropper stands in the floor like a stake.

How each panel finding is addressed:
- Hairline figures: the outline is 6px at 1x, the brim 8px, the body a filled flat, and the cap is bigger (128 units tall overall). In the 480x270 render both painters, the blue tank and the orange roller read clearly.
- Yellow on light surfaces: every team-paint group goes through one SVG filter, `#key`, which dilates the alpha by 2px into black. So every coat, drip and airbrush speck sits on an ink keyline. The sheet shows yellow working on the cream palette swatch, the eraser rubber, the white text box and the lavender selection. There is no sun.
- Sparse scene: about ten tool props plus jokes that work at the screenshot level (the selection lifted a chunk of "Untitled" and left a white hole in the letters, the eraser rubbed a white band through the U, "fill leaked. outline had a gap.", "curve tool: never finished", a text box that types its own name). This answers the "jokes carried it" note.
- Roller read as a box: it is now a cylinder seen slightly from behind, with a front cap ellipse, a grey axle hub, a receding body, nap ticks and a wire frame running to the hub, on a 96-unit handle.
- Sprayer tank over the torso: it is redrawn so the grip is at the hand and everything sits ahead of the body. The reservoir is on top of the gun body, so nothing overlaps the shirt.
- Hang-lines: removed. Platforms float like pasted selections.
- Crude must read as deliberate: one consistent set of rules (below), with bucket-fill holes kept as a signature.
- Team hues kept out of the structure: the world uses only greys, Paint brown, cream, lavender and crimson. The palette floor leaves out every team hue, so the "palette" has no team colours until players paint it.
rules: Walkable things are tools and have a 5px black pencil outline (the palette strip, pencil, eraser, text box, selection, resize handle). Backdrop props are Paint icons in 4px grey (#9A9A9A) ink with #EEEEEE fill and never look solid. If it is black-lined you can stand on it.

Structure uses only non-team Paint palette colours: greys #4A4A4A/#7F7F7F/#C3C3C3, brown #B97A57, cream #EFE4B0, lavender #C8BFE7 and crimson #880015, with one lighter and one darker facet. Never use blue, orange, pink, green or yellow on a tool.

All team paint goes inside the keyline filter (feMorphology dilate radius 2 to black). Drips, bands, splats and airbrush specks all carry a 2px ink rim, so all five team colours read on any surface value.

Painters are black and white plus exactly two flat team regions, the cap crown and the shirt. Weapons add the sprayer reservoir and nozzle tip, and the roller sleeve. Everything else is fixed colour. Use a 6px line at 1x, leave a couple of white bucket-fill hole pixels per region, and do not add detail.
Weapons sit in front of the hand and never over the torso. The roller is always drawn as a cylinder (front cap ellipse, hub and receding body), not a rectangle.

Every new prop needs a Paint-artefact joke that reads in a still: a fill leaking through a gap, a selection that leaves a background-coloured hole, an eraser band, an unfinished curve tool, a text box that types what it is. Grey text annotations are allowed in the backdrop only.
Everything renders aliased (shape-rendering crispEdges) with mouse-wobble polylines: about 1.4px jitter on structure, about 0.6px on characters and none on brims and feet.
variants.self:
Strengths:
- The scene is far denser than round 1 and reads as "made of Paint" at a glance.
- At 480x270 both painters, the sprayer tank, the roller and all the paint are legible.
- The keyline filter really does fix yellow and green on the cream, white and lavender surfaces, as the 18-chip swatch grid (6 surfaces x 3 pairs) shows.
- The tint mask panel makes team-region separability explicit.

Weaknesses:
- The palette-strip floor is busy: a grid of muted swatches competes a little with the floor paint. In-game it may want lower contrast, or a single swatch row with a plain base.
- In the scene the roller is small (about 48px), so it reads as "drum on a stick" rather than a decorator's roller unless you zoom in.
- Grey icon props in the sky float without justification beyond "they're icons".
- The selection's hole joke on the faint "Untitled" is subtle and may need a darker ghost value to land.
- Text-box paint drips across the word "platform"; I left it in as a joke, but it is noisier than it needs to be.
- The SMIL caret and marching ants only animate in a browser; the PNGs show one frame.

Icon props scattered in the sky with no grounding (bucket, brush, magnifier, spray can all at similar weight). Cut to two or three, or cluster them so the backdrop reads less like a clip-art sheet.
The roller at in-scene scale. About 48px still reads as 'drum on a stick'. The sleeve needs to be larger relative to the body, or the handle shorter.
variants.verdict: This is the strongest structural idea so far for making Paint.exe maximalism into a level grammar, not just a look. Tools as terrain gives every platform a joke and an identity, and it gives a rule players can learn: black-lined means solid. The keyline filter and the no-team-hue rule for structure are solid production rules and should go into the final style whatever else is chosen. Execution is good but over-dense. The double palette-strip floor and the big ghost 'Untitled' lower contrast at 480x270, so split-screen readability is the weak point. In the quarter pane the painters still read, but the roller is marginal. Cost is moderate: each tool platform is a bespoke sprite, though they tile simply (eraser, text box and selection are 9-slice-able rectangles; the pencil ramp is a one-off). Recommendation: carry the rules and the eraser, selection and text-box platforms forward, tone down the floor and backdrop by about 40%, and make it the base level vocabulary for the combined style.

identity.reason: The most ownable idea in the set, with no ready comparison. Paint's own tools become the terrain: the eraser block, the marching-ants selection, the 'platform|' text box and the pencil ramp. Every platform carries a joke and a learnable rule (black-lined means solid). The figures keep round-1's soul. At 480x270 the two-row palette floor and the ghost 'Untitled' are too loud, and the roller is marginal. Both are tuning problems, not concept problems.

production.reason: The strongest level-grammar idea: platforms made of Paint tools (eraser, marching-ants selection, a 'platform|' text box, the pencil ramp) give each arena signature terrain, and most of these 9-slice cheaply. Execution hurts readability: the two-row palette floor is a high-contrast checkerboard that fights the paint, the giant 'Untitled' smudges the mid-frame, and the roller is marginal. Harvest it as a set of special platforms, not as a base style.

player.reason: The strongest level-grammar idea. The tools are the terrain: an eraser, a marching-ants selection, a text box that types 'platform|' and a pencil ramp. It also gives a learnable rule (black outline = solid). It is very screenshot-able and the most 'Paint.exe' at first glance. In the small render, the two-row palette-strip floor is a checkerboard that fights floor paint, and the giant grey 'Untitled' muddies the middle band. Its crimson swatches sit near the orange and pink teams. Tone it down about 40% and it is excellent.

variants.name: Black Canvas
variants.brief: Someone bucket-filled the background black. Black or very dark charcoal canvas, chunky white and grey mouse-drawn lines for the world, mid-grey or dark-grey slabs with a light top edge. Characters are box-heads with white faces and thick black-and-white outlines. Paint is fully saturated and luminous against the dark, with yellow, pink and green tested too. Background gags drawn in dim grey pencil. It should feel like the same game at night, still crude.
variants.one_liner: Black Canvas: the Paint.exe painters at night. A bucket-filled black canvas has chunky white pencil top edges on charcoal slabs, white box-heads with a black core line and a white keyline, and saturated paint with a black rim and a lighter glint, so even dark blue glows.
variants.changed: Compared with the round-1 Paint.exe concept, the canvas is now near-black (#121212). The world is mid-grey and dark-grey slabs with a grey pencil outline, a chunky 6px white top edge on every walkable surface and a darker lip band under it. The figure-read finding is addressed with a 6px black core line inside a white keyline. Faces are white, bodies are filled, and the cap crown and brim are bigger. The eyes were moved off the head outline, where one had been swallowed by it. The figures stay legible as white-and-colour blocks in the 480x270 render. The yellow-contrast finding is addressed by drawing a 7px black rim under every paint band, drip and splat, with a lighter-tint glint strip on top. The glint is derivable from the runtime tint and is what lets #0634CC read on dark grey. There is no sun any more: the moon is dim grey with an eraser bite, so no team hue appears in the world. The roller is now a capsule-outlined cylinder with a grey end disc, an axle, nap stripes and a bent wire frame, so it no longer reads as a box. The sprayer is split into a backpack tank (whose window shows team colour) and a two-handed wand joined by a hose, so nothing sits over the torso. The hang-lines are gone and the platforms simply float. For the sparseness finding, the background now carries about 15 dim-grey pencil gags: a tipped-over giant paint-bucket cursor captioned "tolerance: 100% (sorry)" (the in-world reason the canvas is black), a moon rubbed out a bit, an erased "sun.bmp (it is night now)", a cloud still selected with marching ants, an empty text box with a caret, a pencil cursor still drawing the moon, a "plane (not to scale)", a horizon city line with dim windows, a sleeping owl, eyes in an alley, a "bulb.bmp not found" lamp post, a "save changes to untitled.bmp? [no]" dialog, ctrl+z scrawl, and "floor.bmp (do not paint)" on the floor face. All gags are kept far below paint in value. The sheet shows idle, run+sprayer and jump for both teams; a large sprayer with its tank; a large roller; an actual-size lineup of all five team colours with the 52x120 collision box; and swatches for blue/orange, pink/green and blue/yellow (unpainted, A, B and overpaint), with pink/green also shown on the darker floor slab. About 48% of the walkable tops are painted, split between the teams. rules: The canvas is bucket-filled black (#121212). The world is only greys: slab bodies #4B4B4B (platform) and #303030 (floor), outlined in a 4px #9A9A9A pencil line, with a 6px #E6E6E6 top edge on every surface you can stand on. No team hue ever appears in structure.

Every paint mark (band, drip, splat, droplet) gets a black rim about 3px wider than the fill, drawn first. A short glint strip at 55% toward white sits on top of each band. The glint is computed from the tint, so runtime recolouring still works.

Draw characters with each line twice on the same wobble: a white keyline 5px wider underneath, then a 6px black core. Faces are white. Team colour goes only on the cap crown, shirt, tank window, nozzle and roller sleeve, each as its own flat fill.

A background gag is a dim-grey pencil drawing (#2C2C2C to #4E4E4E) with a deadpan Comic Sans caption about Paint itself (a file name, a tool, an undo). It must stay darker than any slab, and it never overlaps a player's path or the paint.

Weapons read by silhouette. The sprayer is a backpack tank, a hose and a two-handed wand held clear of the torso. The roller is a capsule-shaped cylinder with an end disc, an axle and nap stripes, never a rectangle.
Keep it aliased: shape-rendering crispEdges, square pixel specks for the airbrush, and bucket fills that stop 2-3px short of the line so a few black canvas pixels show through.
variants.self: Strongest: paint and characters read well, including at 480x270. Saturated paint on near-black with a black rim plus glint looks luminous, and dark blue survives because of the glint. The white keyline makes the figures pop more than in round 1. The roller now reads as a roller, and the backpack sprayer keeps the torso clear. The swatches show all three pairs holding contrast, yellow and blue included. Weaker: the dim gags carry the maximalism only at full size. At quarter-pane they fade into texture, which is correct for gameplay but means the joke density isn't visible in a small screenshot. The sky is still emptier than a true maximalist piece. The sprayer hose is mostly hidden behind the legs in the scene. The pink/green dark-floor swatch barely differs from the platform slab. Blue and dark-blue paint is the weakest pair and depends on the glint. At 126 px the characters run slightly over the 100-120 px brief because of the bigger cap.
keep: A black rim drawn under every paint band, drip and splat, plus a glint strip computed from the tint. This is the most valuable idea here: runtime recolouring still works, and it rescues dark blue and yellow on any background. Carry it into the final style whatever colour the canvas is.

The double-stroked characters: a wider white keyline under the black core line on the same wobble. At 480x270 the figures pop as white-and-colour blocks, a clear improvement over the round-1 thin stick figures.
The chunky light top edge on every walkable surface, so what you can stand on reads instantly as structure, separate from decoration.
A rule that no team hue ever appears in structure. The round-1 yellow sun and orange paint bucket broke this, and here the moon is grey.

The roller redrawn as a capsule cylinder with an end disc, an axle and nap stripes, and the sprayer split into a backpack tank (its window showing the ammo) and a two-handed wand. Both read by silhouette and keep the torso clear.
Background gags kept strictly below slab value, captioned deadpan about Paint itself. 'tolerance: 100% (sorry)' is an in-world reason for the art style, which is a great device.
Floating platforms without the hang-lines, which are cleaner.
Black Canvas as a night stage or alternate-palette arena under the same rules, rather than as the default look.
drop: Making black the default canvas. The white-page MS Paint identity is the author's original charm, and on black the style drifts toward generic neon-on-dark indie. Use it as a stage variant instead.
The dark floor slab (#303030) is nearly the same value as the canvas and the platform, so the pink/green dark-floor swatch barely differs from the platform slab. Raise it or drop it.
Sky gags that only work at full size: at quarter-pane they become noise or texture. Keep fewer, bigger gags, or accept them as texture and stop counting on them for the maximalism.
The hose hidden behind the legs in the run pose: route it over the shoulder, or drop it in-game.
The extra height from the bigger cap, which pushes the figures to 126 px. Trim it back inside the 120 px collision box.
Off-screen corner splats that look stray at the pane edge (the left wall).
variants.verdict: This is solid execution and the strongest technical answer so far to the contrast and figure-read findings. Paint glows, both teams and all five colours hold up, and the figures read at 480x270. As the base style, though, it gives up part of what the author loves: a white MS Paint page with crude doodles. On black it becomes a "night mode" that looks more polished and more like other neon indie games, and the maximalist gags fade to texture at gameplay scale. Take its mechanics (black-rimmed glinting paint, keylined figures, light walkable top edges, no team hue in structure, silhouette weapons) into the final combined style. Keep black only as an alternate night arena.

identity.reason: Technically excellent: glint-on-black paint and double-stroked figures. But it trades the white MS Paint page for a neon-on-dark look that has many comparisons, and its gags fade to texture. Keep it as a night stage variant only.

production.reason: Technically strong: rimmed paint with a glint that survives tinting, white-keylined figures that pop, a light walkable top edge. It loses the white-page identity, though, and drifts toward neon-on-dark indie, and its maximal gags fade to texture at quarter pane. Ideal as one night arena under the shared rules.

player.reason: Technically strong: rim plus glint makes paint glow, and the keylined figures pop. But a black canvas trades away the white MS Paint page identity for a generic neon-on-dark look, and its gags fade to texture. It is right as an alternate night stage, not as the base.

variants.name: Default Landscape
variants.brief: The classic picture every kid drew in MS Paint: a bucket-filled green hill, a filled sky, a yellow sun in the corner with line rays, "m" birds, a brown box house with a triangle roof, all with leaky bucket fills and gaps. Use the default 28-colour palette, but keep team hues out of the world: the sky must not be team blue, so use cyan/teal or very pale, or leave it white with a crayon-like scribble. Push the world to a lighter, lower-saturation version so paint wins. Slabs need a clear dark top edge.
variants.one_liner: The picture every kid drew in MS Paint (sky strip, corner sun, m-birds, box house, lollipop tree, labelled 'by matt (age 7)'), chalked pale so the keylined team paint is the loudest thing on screen.
variants.changed:
Round 1 was a grey, empty canvas held up by its jokes. This version fills the world with the default-landscape clichés: a teal crayon sky strip with the white gap below it, a quarter sun in the corner, m-birds, clouds, a far hill with a brown box house (a leaky bucket fill spills out by the door, labelled "oops (gap)"), a lollipop tree, a stick dog, a picket fence, a kite, flowers, and a signature. All of it uses the 28-colour palette pushed toward white. One running joke ties it together and makes the crudeness read as deliberate: the kid labels everything in the same grey hand with arrows ("the sky", "sun (NOT a team)", "flat cloud (for standing)").

How it answers the panel:
(1) Figures read at 480x270. The lines are 6px (up from 3-4), the shirt and cap are filled and larger, and the brim is 8px. Both players are still clearly legible in scene_small.png.
(2) Yellow on light surfaces. Every piece of team paint (bands, drips, splats, droplets, airbrush mist) gets a black keyline: a stroked copy is drawn underneath the flat copy, so overlapping pieces merge into one outline. The sheet shows all three pairs (blue/orange, pink/green, blue/yellow) on all three walkable surfaces (hill, plank, flat cloud). The sun is now pale cream with a brown outline, not yellow.
(3) The scene is no longer sparse.
(4) The sprayer reservoir moved to a backpack tank with a team-colour window, joined by a hose to a gun held in front, so nothing overlaps the torso. The roller is now a cylinder seen at 3/4: team sleeve, grey end cap and axle, and roll-curl lines. The hang-lines are gone.
(5) Every walkable top has a 6px black edge; nothing else in the world does.
(6) No team hue appears in the structural colours. The sheet's palette box crosses out the team-only chips and shows the chalked-down world swatches.

Coverage is about 50% of walkable tops, split blue and orange.

variants.self:
Strong on the brief. Unlike round 1, the scene now reads as deliberately maximal. The keyline rule fixes yellow and green on every surface, as the blue/yellow and pink/green rows of the sheet show. Both players and both weapons stay legible at 480x270. The kid-label joke gives the crudeness a consistent voice.

Weaknesses:
- The teal zigzag sky is fairly regular and a little loud for a strip meant to recede.
- The airbrush mist near P1's nozzle clumps into a dense patch rather than a fine spray.
- The grey labels are effectively unreadable at quarter-pane size. They are flavour, not information, and would likely need to go or be enlarged in-game.
- Keylining all paint adds visual weight to blue, which arguably did not need it.
- The scene only shows the blue/orange draw; the other pairs are proven only on the sheet.
- The white gap between the sky strip and the hills is a real empty band, intentional as the kid-drawing joke but it costs some of the maximalism.
keep: The black-edge rule: only walkable tops get the thick black line, and every other world line is a 3px muted pencil. It is the most useful gameplay idea in the set. You can see it work on the floating planks and the flat cloud even at 480x270.

A black keyline underlay under all team paint, drawn as a stroked copy behind the flat copy so overlapping pieces merge into one outline. The swatch grid shows it rescues yellow and green on every pale surface.

Team hues are reserved: the default 28-colour palette chips are crossed out as 'team only', and the world uses chalked-down versions of the other chips. It reads as a rule a player can feel, and it is cheap to enforce in data.
The sun is pale cream with a brown outline, labelled 'sun (NOT a team)'. It fixes a real colour clash and makes a joke of the fix.
The sprayer is a backpack tank with a team-colour paint window, joined by a hose to a gun held in front. The ammo readout lives on the character, and nothing covers the torso.
The roller is a 3/4 cylinder with a team sleeve and a grey end cap. It is much more readable than round 1's box.
6px limbs, a filled shirt, and an 8px cap brim. These sizes make the figures survive the quarter pane.
Leaky bucket-fill details, at most one deliberate 'mistake' per backdrop object (the 'oops (gap)' spill by the house).
The 'by matt (age 7)' signature as one corner gag. One is charming.
The kid-drawing backdrop clichés (box house, lollipop tree, m-birds, kite, picket fence), kept low and pale behind the floor. They fill the emptiness of round 1 without competing.
drop: The kid's labels on every object ('the sky', 'tree', 'dog', 'birds', 'my house'). At 480x270 they are grey mush, and across a whole level they turn into noise. Keep at most one or two per stage as easter eggs, or only the signature.
The regular teal zigzag sky strip. It is the loudest non-team element on screen and reads as a border pattern, not a sky. Use a looser, sparser crayon scribble, or put it at much lower opacity.
The empty white band between the sky strip and the hills. It brings back round 1's sparseness across the middle third of the frame, which is exactly where the floating platforms sit.

Foreground slabs filled with the same chalk as the backdrop hill. The ramp vanishes, the right ledge reads as scenery, and only the black edge tells you it is solid. Walkable bodies need a distinct, slightly heavier fill, like the plank tan.
The flat cloud as a platform material. Its lavender-white fill nearly matches the background, so the slab disappears below the paint. Either give it a body or drop it.
The dense clumped airbrush patch at the nozzle. Thin it to sparse specks so the spray reads as an arc rather than a blob.
Keylines on blue. Blue does not need the extra weight, so consider keylining only the light team hues, or a thinner keyline for dark ones, to keep the draw visually even.
variants.verdict: This variation solves round 1's real problems: the empty grey canvas, figures too thin to read, and yellow failing on light surfaces. It does so with rules that are cheap for a solo developer and that feel like Paint itself rather than another style. The black-edge-means-walkable rule, keylined team paint and team-only palette chips are the three ideas the final style should inherit, and the backpack-tank sprayer and cylinder roller belong in it too. The execution has holes. The labels are unreadable at quarter-pane size and would get tiresome over a full level. The zigzag sky is louder than anything except the paint. The white band across the middle brings back some of the emptiness it set out to fix. The foreground slabs (ramp, right ledge, flat cloud) share their fill with the backdrop, so the black edge does all the work and the ramp reads as a floating orange stick. As a whole look it is a strong 7. As a source of rules for the combined style it is one of the most useful variations. Take the rules and the weapon designs, cut the joke to a single signature, and give walkable bodies their own fill.

identity.reason: Very Paint-native and ownable through its 'by matt (age 7)' voice. It has the useful rule that black edges mean walkable. The teal zigzag sky is the loudest non-team element, the labels turn to mush at quarter pane, and the foreground slabs share the hill's fill, so the ramp reads as a floating stick.

production.reason: Charming, and very Paint, with good rules (only walkable tops get a black edge, team chips crossed out). But the walkable bodies share fill with the backdrop hill, so the ramp floats and the cloud slab vanishes, and the zigzag sky is the loudest non-team element. The labels on everything turn to mush and get tiresome across levels. It works as a single 'kid's drawing' arena theme.

player.reason: Most nostalgic and closest to the author's crude soul. The black edge only on walkable tops is a great rule, and 'sun (NOT a team)' is a good gag. Against it: the loud teal zigzag sky strip, an empty white middle band, and foreground slabs (the ramp, the flat cloud) sharing the backdrop's fill so they vanish. The labels are mush at quarter pane.

variants.name: Airbrush Everything
variants.brief: Everything is shaded with the Paint airbrush tool: square-pixel speckle clouds for shadows, grime, depth and ambience; spray-can tags on walls; speckled gradients on slabs; a speckle haze in the sky. The sprayer's mist is the airbrush tool, so the weapon and the world share a texture. Keep team paint as solid bucket fill, with speckle only at its edges, so the score stays crisp and the world stays speckled.
variants.one_liner: A greyscale world shaded only with Paint's square-speck airbrush (sky haze, grime gradients, cast shadows, spray-can tags), where team paint is the only colour: flat bucket fill with a black keyline and speckle only at its edges.
variants.changed:
Round 1 was white canvas with quiet pencil doodles. Here every non-team surface is airbrushed. The sky has a speckle haze that thins toward the horizon, and the clouds are bucket-filled holes in it. Each slab is speckled darker toward its underside. Floating platforms cast speckle shadows onto the backdrop, which replaces the hang-lines that cluttered round 1. There is an airbrush-shaded skyline and a back wall covered in spray tags: "ctrl+z", "C/W", a sprayed box-head painter, "was here", a crown, an arrow, and "est. 2022" on the step face. The sprayer's mist uses the same speck as the world.

- Sun: it is now the white "eraser tool" disc, never yellow.

- Sprayer: the tank sits forward of the grip, so it clears the torso.

Shade only with the airbrush: square specks of 3px (2px for overspray), with density running from 0 to 1. Slabs get darker toward their underside. Anything floating casts a speckle shadow on whatever is behind it. Never use smooth gradients or blur.

Characters use a 6px pencil, a flat team fill on the cap crown and body, a white head, 5px square eyes, a bar mouth and a 62px black brim. There are no specks on team regions. The only speckle on a figure is a light grey brim shadow on the face and a speckle contact shadow, which is dropped when airborne.

Weapons sit forward of the body. Team colour on a weapon goes only in clearly bounded regions (the sprayer's window and nozzle, the roller's sleeve), and the sprayer's mist is literally the world's airbrush speck in team colour.

Wall graffiti is the maximalism. Spray tags go on walls and step faces in black, white or grey, with a hard pencil core, overspray specks and an occasional drip. Text-tool jokes about the Paint tools themselves (bucket, eraser, airbrush, dot counts) go in the sky and margins in dark grey.

Keep the backdrop lighter and lower-contrast than the playfield. The sky haze thins to bare canvas by mid-height so figures on platforms sit on near-white, and the playable slabs are the darkest structural greys.
variants.self:
Strong points:
- The concept reads as one consistent system: the dots are the world, the flat colour is the score.
- At 480x270 both figures, the mist arc and every painted top are clearly legible. Blue and orange pop hard against the greyscale world.
- The swatches cover all three draws. The keyline A/B swatch shows yellow vanishing on light grey without the keyline and holding with it.
- The joke system (bucket cloud, eraser sun, real dot count) makes the crudeness feel intentional.
- Coverage is about 50% of walkable tops, split between the teams.

Weaknesses:
- The speckle sky is busy, and in motion it might shimmer or read as noise and compression artefacts. A real implementation would want a fixed baked texture, not per-frame specks.
- The roller's wire crank is small, so at quarter size the roller reads as a "cylinder on a stick" rather than an obvious decorator's roller.
- The right-hand sky between y 250 and 450 is still fairly empty.
- The labels use Comic Sans from a generic font stack, which falls back differently on other machines.
keep: The core system: a greyscale world where team paint is the only colour. Blue and orange pop hard even at 480x270, and the score reads instantly.
Speckle-only shading with slabs darkening toward the underside. It gives depth without leaving MS Paint, and it can be baked once per tile.
Speckle cast shadows under floating platforms instead of round 1's hang-lines. Cleaner, and it also grounds the platforms in space.
The sprayer's mist uses the world's airbrush speck in team colour, so weapon and world share one texture. The best idea in the set.
Speckle only at the edges of team paint, flat bucket fill in the middle, which keeps coverage crisp.
A black keyline under team paint (pink, green and yellow swatches all hold against grey slabs).
The white eraser-tool sun and the bucket-hole cloud. Tool-joke props make the crudeness read as intentional, so keep them on the dark-grey text-tool layer.
Spray tags on walls and step faces in greyscale (ctrl+z, C/W, est. 2022, the box-head 'was here'). Maximalism that never competes with team hues.
The rounded roller tube with an end-cap ellipse, and the sprayer tank sitting forward of the grip.
The figure spec: 6px pencil, a flat-filled body and cap, a white head, a 62px brim, and a contact shadow dropped when airborne.
drop: A uniform speckle haze across the whole sky. It is the busiest layer, it fights the mist texture (both are 'dots'), and it will shimmer or read as compression noise in motion. Thin it to a band near the top, or use a few baked patches.
Speckle on the mid-ground wall at nearly the same value as the playfield floor. The step and wall plane run together with the floor band, so separate the values more.
Footer and caption text at body size, such as the dot-count footer and 'sun (eraser tool, size L)'. Illegible at a quarter pane. Keep the jokes for the capsule and the title, not for every level.
A roller wire crank too thin to survive at 0.3x. Thicken it, or accept 'cylinder on a stick'.
Leaning on the keyline alone for yellow. On light grey it only partly rescues it, so yellow still needs the slab top darkened or a cap of the team's darker shade.
Comic Sans fallback labels from a font stack. Bake text as bitmaps if any is kept.
variants.verdict: This is the strongest systemic idea in the Paint.exe family. 'The world is grey dots, the score is flat colour' gives the crude art a rule that also does gameplay work: coverage is unmistakable at quarter size. The mist-equals-airbrush link is a real design rhyme. Execution is good but over-applied. The full-sky haze and the uniformly speckled wall make the frame noisy, compete with the mist, and will likely shimmer in motion. The walkable slabs and the backdrop sit too close in value at the bottom of the frame. Figures read at 480x270 but are small, and the sprayer's grey body still overlaps the torso in the run pose. It is cheap for a solo dev if specks are baked into tile textures and never generated per frame. Carry the colour rule, the cast shadows, the mist texture, the edge-only speckle and the greyscale tags forward, and use airbrush density as a value tool, not a blanket.

identity.reason: The tightest system: the world is grey speckle and the score is flat colour. The sprayer mist is the world's own airbrush, and speckle cast shadows replace the hang-lines. Wall tags give maximalism with no hue competition. The look is distinct and stays recognisably the author's figures. The full-sky haze is noisy and will shimmer in motion, and the wall and floor values merge at the bottom of the frame.

production.reason: The best systemic idea: a grey dotted world with flat-colour score, and the mist using the world's own speck. Cast speckle shadows replace the hang-lines nicely, and the specks bake cheaply into tiles. As drawn, though, the full-sky haze is noisy at quarter pane, will shimmer in motion and competes with the mist. The wall and floor values run together at the bottom of the frame. Use airbrush as a value tool layered onto the winner, not as the whole look.

player.reason: Strongest single rule: the world is grey dots and the score is flat colour. Mist made from the same airbrush texture as the world is a real design rhyme, and the speckle cast shadows replace the hang-lines nicely. The full-sky speckle haze is noisy, will shimmer in motion and competes with the mist. The wall and floor values run together at the bottom. Use it as a shading technique, not a blanket.

variants.self:
**What works.**
- At 480x270 the figures and paint read clearly. That is the main win over round 1.
- The keyline makes yellow and green solid on white and on light grey, as the swatches show.
- The roller now reads as a roller, and the sprayer no longer covers the shirt.
- The jokes follow a few consistent rules (faces on everything, the wrong-brush cloud, the leaked fill), so the crudeness reads as intentional.

**Weaknesses.**
- The upper third is still fairly airy. The light-grey doodles are kept quiet on purpose, so this is maximal in jokes more than in density.
- The fat outline eats into small interiors. Cap crowns show only a band of team colour at small size, and the run pose gets cramped where the arms cross the gun.
- The platform shade stroke can read as a double outline.
- The large sprayer is chunky and pipe-like, more 'paint cannon' than pressure sprayer.
- Overlapping 10 px ink at the joints can blob together. That fits the brief, but it costs fine pose detail.
keep: Black keyline under every paint mark (6 px fatter than the paint). It is the single best fix in the set: yellow and green hold on white and on light grey, and the swatches show all three pairings work
Fat 9-10 px foreground strokes on the characters. At 480x270 the box head, flat cap and team-colour shirt still read as a person on a team, which is a clear improvement on round 1's pencil figures
A two-tier ink rule: fat black for anything you can collide with or play, light-grey #C3C3C3 for background doodles. Playable space separates from decoration at a glance
A world limited to black, two greys and white, with team hue only in paint and in the cap crown, shirt, tank window, nozzle and roller sleeve. That keeps the paint the loudest thing on screen
The rebuilt roller: a cylinder with a grey end cap and a pole going into that cap, leaving a flat trail. It reads instantly
Sprayer tank forward of the grip at hip height, never crossing the shirt
Two-dot face on every prop (clouds, sun, balloon, houses), as a cheap and consistent joke system
'wrong brush' crossed-out hairline cloud and the 'sun (grey. yellow is a team)' label: dry, self-aware jokes that are Paint-native
Platforms supported by trestles or a ladder instead of hang-lines, plus 'floats. don't ask' for the one that floats
Airbrush mist turning into keylined droplets that land as a splat, which tells the projectile's story in one image
The actual-size row on the sheet, kept as a standing QA check for every future variation
drop: The 'gap in outline. fill leaked.' leak shape. It renders as an ambiguous grey hand or blob hanging under the platform, not as bucket-fill spill. Either make it an unmistakable flood-fill shape running into the sky, or cut it
The 'oops' eraser hole. The small black-outlined houses beside it read as foreground props rather than an erased patch, so the joke does not land
The light-grey background houses and fence behind the left platform. They tangle with its trestles, and at quarter pane the support structure becomes grey noise
The dark-grey shade stroke inside every platform's bottom edge. At small size it reads as a double outline; use one shade, or none
Interior cracks (zigzags) on the ground fill. They are visible clutter at 480x270 and add nothing
The overscaled pipe-like sprayer barrel. Keep the tank placement, but shorten and slim the barrel so it reads as a pressure sprayer rather than a cannon
The airy upper third. If this is meant to be maximalism it needs more grey doodle density, or else accept that it is really 'fat-brush minimalism with jokes'
variants.verdict: This is the strongest readability pass on the Paint.exe direction so far, and it fixes most of the round-1 panel findings. The 10 px brush makes the box-head flat-cap figures survive quarter pane. The black keyline under paint solves the yellow and green problem on light surfaces outright. The roller and sprayer now read as what they are. It still feels like the author's own MS Paint art, just drawn with a thumb-sized marker, and it would be cheap for a solo developer to produce (one stroke size, flat fills, a three-grey world). It falls short in two ways. First, it is not maximal: the top third is empty, and the density lives in the labels, not the picture. Second, two of its jokes (the leaked fill and 'oops') render ambiguously, and a joke that has to be explained reads as unfinished, not deliberate. The grey background houses also tangle with the left platform's trestles. Execution is about 7/10. The potential is higher, perhaps 8.5/10, as the readability backbone of the final style. The keyline rule, the fat-stroke characters and the black-vs-grey ink tiers should go into the final combined style almost unchanged, paired with a busier sibling variation that supplies the maximalist density.

identity.reason: The clearest figures and paint at quarter pane. It is cheap (one brush, three greys) and plainly the author's drawing at marker scale, and the faces-on-props joke system is charming. It is not maximal: the top third is airy. The leak and 'oops' jokes render ambiguously, and the grey background houses tangle with the trestles.

production.reason: The clearest figures and paint at quarter pane, and the cheapest rule set: one fat stroke, three greys and a keyline under all paint. The two-tier ink (fat black means playable, light grey means backdrop) works at a glance. The faces on every prop and the 'wrong brush' cloud form a scalable joke system. Weaknesses: the top third is airy, the leak blob and the 'oops' gag are ambiguous, the grey houses tangle with the trestles, and the sprayer reads as a cannon.

player.reason: The best raw readability. 10px strokes make the painters bold at quarter pane, and the two-dot face on every prop is a cheap, charming system. It is cheap to produce. It is not maximal, though: the top third is airy, the leaked-fill gag reads as a grey blob, and the grey houses tangle with the trestles. It belongs in the line-weight spec, not the whole look.

variants.name: Zoom 400%
variants.brief: The canvas was drawn at very low resolution with the mouse, then shown at 400% zoom with nearest-neighbour scaling. The staircase aliasing becomes chunky and visible, and lines are 1 low-res pixel wide (4 px on screen). This is NOT crafted pixel art: there is no shading clusters, no hand-placed anti-aliasing, no outlines chosen for readability. It is wobbly mouse lines and leaky bucket fills that happen to be big. Draw it with <rect> cells on a coarse grid (about 400x225 cells) through a generator script. It should still feel like Paint, not Celeste.
variants.one_liner: A 400x225 MS Paint canvas viewed at 400% with nearest-neighbour scaling. Bresenham mouse lines, bucket fills and airbrush speckle become chunky 4 px cells, and every word is a 3x5 aliased text-tool font. It reads as a game made in Paint, not as pixel art.

variants.verdict: This is a strong variation, and the most production-ready Paint.exe direction so far, mostly because it adds a real value system rather than because of the zoom. Dark-grey walkables with black keylines plus light-grey doodle backdrops let team paint dominate at 480x270, which fixes round 1's washed-out floors and hairline figures. Execution is clean: renders are current, the coats and the mist arc read at a glance, and the jokes are genuinely good, with 'SUN (YELLOW IS TAKEN)' the best of them. The risk is the zoom gimmick itself. The scene still feels like Paint because of the wobble and the doodles, but the character sheet already slides into Celeste-adjacent chunky pixel art, and a hard 4x cell grid will be awkward under scrolling and four-pane scaling. Potential: high, if the final style keeps the value ladder, keylines, coat recipe and jokes and treats the chunky aliasing as texture rather than a literal grid. The pasted box and the orange cloud blob are small execution slips. Blue on #808080 is the weakest pair and survives only because of the keyline.

identity.reason: The best gameplay frame at quarter pane. Risks: a literal 4x grid fights scrolling and four-pane scaling, it drifts toward generic pixel art up close, and an orange blob in a cloud breaks the hue rule.

production.reason: The best gameplay frame in the set. For a solo non-artist it is the most authorable: whole cells, Bresenham lines, flood fill and a fixed coat recipe are all procedural and repeatable across 4+ arenas. The best jokes are here too: SUN (YELLOW IS TAKEN), LAST COAT WINS, the marquee cloud. Risks: a literal 400x225 grid fights scrolling and non-integer pane scaling, the orange blob in the top-left cloud breaks the hue rule, and the sprayer is small.

Painters use a 6-7px pencil line. The shirt and cap crown are flat team colour and the head is flat white. The face is two 5x6 dot eyes and one mouth line. The brim is an 8px bar. Held weapons sit fully ahead of the torso. Painters are never drawn as clip art, because the clash between the two styles is the joke.
Text-tool notes are quiet grey Comic, at most 2-3 per screen, and they caption a pasting mistake ("transparent selection: OFF", "<- stretched to fit"). They are never UI.
variants.self:
The scene delivers the brief and has the density round 1 lacked. Each clip-art gag reads in a screenshot. P1 is mid-run with the sprayer, a stream that breaks into droplets, and a landing splat. P2 pushes a roller that now reads as a drum, leaving an orange trail on platform B. There is one ramp and a step, and roughly half the walkable tops are painted, split between the teams. At 480x270 both painters and all paint still read: white head, team shirt, black keyline. The stretched clip-art supports make the platforms look held up rather than floating.

Weaknesses:
- The washed clip art is still the largest-area element. The globe and trophy boxes pull some attention at quarter-pane size. A stronger wash, or a cooler and lower-contrast wallpaper, would push them back further.
- The painters are still small at 116 px, as the brief requires. P2's facing direction is carried mainly by the brim.
- The keyline makes paint look slightly sticker-like next to round 1's looser drips.
- Clip-art density would need care in a real level so it does not hide a platform's edges.

The sheet proves all three team pairs on the slab and on the bare wall, shows all five hues at actual size, and states the clip-art rule.
keep: The two-layer rule: anything a player touches or scores on (painters, slabs, paint) is aliased Paint, and anything that is only scenery is something else. This rule is what makes crude read as a choice. Of all the variations, it does the most for 'deliberate, not unfinished'.

A black keyline under every coat of paint (stroke it black, then fill it flat on top). It makes yellow hold on grey and on pale walls, and it separates paint from the backdrop at quarter-pane size. This is worth carrying into any final style.
Darker slab grey #8E8E8E, compared with round 1's pale grey. Both team hues sit on it with a clear value gap, and the slabs read as solid ground.
Props that do structural work, replacing round 1's hang-lines: a stretched cabinet, plant or trophy holds up a slab. Platforms look supported, and the stretch itself is the gag.
Heavier painters: 6-7px pencil, filled shirt, bigger cap crown, 8px brim and bigger eyes. At 480x270 they still read as a white head, a team shirt and a cap.
The roller redrawn as a 3/4 drum with a fuzzy nap, plus a sprayer whose tank sits ahead of the grip. Both weapon silhouettes now read.

Editor-artifact gags used sparingly: one marching-ants selection with 8 handles per screen, and the 'transparent selection: OFF' white boxes. These are cheap, flat and very Paint-specific, and they fit any Paint-based variant.
Quiet grey Comic text notes, at most 2-3 per screen, that caption a mistake ('<- stretched to fit'). They carry over from round 1's 'do not move this cloud' and still land.
Excluding team hues from every prop and structure colour: a tan sun and a silver trophy.
Stated as a principle: a mid-value, low-saturation wallpaper instead of pure white, so that white objects (heads, boxes) can separate from it.
drop: Glossy gradient clip art as the main backdrop language. Each prop is a polished vector asset the author did not draw and cannot cheaply produce in volume. Clip-art packs bring licensing risk, and drawing them is the expensive kind of art that Paint.exe was meant to avoid. If kept, limit it to 3-5 reusable props per level, not 20.

Clip-art density at this level. Even washed back, the backdrop is the largest-area element. At quarter-pane size the globe, trophy and lightbulb boxes compete with the painters, and P2 on platform B nearly merges with the busy band behind him.

Large white leftover boxes behind high-contrast props (the globe, top left, and the trophy column). At quarter-pane size they are the brightest rectangles on screen apart from the painters' heads. Use them at most once per screen and keep them small.
Pasting the same prop twice where it reads as accidental repetition rather than a joke (the WORLD'S #1 BOSS mug). Players will not notice it as a gag in motion.
Office beige as the only wallpaper colour for the whole game. It reads as dull and dated across a full match. Keep the idea of a non-white wall, but vary it by level.
Losing round 1's pure-white Paint canvas and the canvas border. That border was the most immediately recognisable 'this is MS Paint' cue, and this variation drifts toward 'office desktop' instead.
variants.verdict: This is the strongest framing yet for why the art is crude. The rule "anything a player touches is Paint, the scenery is pasted clip art" turns the crudeness into a joke with a clear target. The execution is good: the paint keyline, the darker slabs, the heavier figures and the prop-held platforms are all real improvements over round 1, and they work in any Paint-family style. Two problems hold it back. The backdrop now does too much: at 480x270 the clip-art layer is the busiest and largest element, and the white boxes and gloss pull the eye from players in a split-screen pane. It also moves the art away from the author's own crude drawing toward polished stock art, which is costly for a solo developer to make or license and dilutes the Paint.exe identity. Harvest the rules (two layers, keyline, darker slab, structural props, selection-handle gags) and a few pasted props per level. Do not adopt glossy clip art as the default backdrop.

identity.reason: The cleverest 'deliberate, not unfinished' framing: crude Paint is what you touch, pasted clip art is the scenery. In practice the glossy stock art becomes the identity, and it is not the author's drawing. It is costly or risky to license, and the beige wall loses the white Paint canvas. At quarter pane the props compete with the players.

production.reason: A great 'deliberate' framing (anything touched is Paint, scenery is pasted), and structural props replace the hang-lines. But glossy clip art is exactly the art a solo non-artist cannot produce cheaply or license safely, the beige wall is dull, and the white boxes compete at quarter pane. Harvest the selection-handle gag and 2-3 stretched props at most.

player.reason: The clearest justification for the crudeness: the Paint layer is what you touch, and clip art is pasted scenery. Pasted props holding up the platforms are a good gag. The backdrop is the largest-area element, though, and its white boxes compete with the painters at quarter pane. It also costs the solo developer polished stock art, and it drifts from the white Paint canvas toward office desktop.

variants.name: Pencil Purist
variants.brief: Closest to the author's original sprite sheet: pure white canvas, the 1-px pencil tool only for the world (black and grey), almost no background, flat empty space as in the original. The ONLY fill colour in the whole game is team paint and the team-coloured cap and shirt. Push this minimalism to look confident rather than unfinished: precise, generous negative space, a few deliberate pencil jokes, very bold paint. Figures may be thicker than 1 px, since they must read at quarter pane.
variants.one_liner: Pencil Purist: a white canvas drawn only with the black and grey pencil, where the only fill colour in the game is team paint and the team cap and shirt. Every wet thing has a pencil rim so yellow reads on white, and a few dry handwritten jokes ("sky: done.", "sun (to scale)", "bird.") say the empty space is on purpose.
variants.changed: Compared with the round-1 Paint.exe concept, the world loses all its fill. The grey bucket-filled slabs, dithered walls, clouds, hills, trees, hang-lines and yellow sun are all gone. Level geometry is now a wobbly 4 px black pencil outline with grey 45-degree pencil hatching inside, which gives the surfaces some value without bringing in a colour. The floor, ramp and step are one continuous hatched block, and the floating platforms have no hang-lines, which fixes the sky clutter. Panel findings addressed: (1) Figures were hairline specks at quarter pane. They now use a 6 px line, a filled team body and a filled team cap, a longer and heavier brim, and a larger white head. Weapons are about 1.3x larger. P1 and P2 both read at 480x270. (2) Yellow failed on white. All paint is now one keylined shape: a 5 px black stroke sits under the fill (paint-order), so a 2.5 px pencil rim shows, and the airbrush specks carry a rim too. The character sheet shows blue/orange, pink/green and blue/yellow on the same hatched block, and yellow holds. The sun is now an empty grey circle, so no yellow is left in the world. (3) The sprayer tank covered the torso. The reservoir is now a rounded team-colour bottle mounted on top of the gun, which is held at arm's length (hands at x=62), so it sits ahead of the body. (4) The roller read as a box. It is now a cylinder in three-quarter view, with a rounded sleeve, an end ellipse with its core and a bent frame on a long pencil handle, and it lays a flat, low-lump trail. (5) "Crude must read as deliberate." Rules are fixed in code: line weights of 6 for people, 4 for the world and 3 for notes; black for things and grey for notes; paint is the only fill and always has a rim. The jokes stay grey and sit outside the play space. (6) Team hues stay out of the world: structure is black, grey and white only. Maximalism is deliberately not attempted, per this brief. Coverage is about 50% of the walkable tops, split blue and orange.
rules: Two inks for the world, black and grey. Black pencil (4 px, wobble amp ~1.2, aliased) draws anything you can stand on or hold. Grey pencil draws notes, hatching and speed marks. The world never has a fill colour; it gets value from 45-degree grey hatching inside an outline.
Paint is the only fill. Team colour appears only as paint on surfaces, the team cap and shirt, the sprayer reservoir and nozzle, and the roller sleeve. Everything else is white canvas or pencil.

Every wet thing gets a pencil rim. Draw each paint shape, drip, droplet and airbrush speck with a black stroke under the fill (paint-order: stroke, 5 px stroke giving a 2.5 px rim). That is what keeps yellow and green readable on white.

People are heavier than the world. Draw figures at a 6 px line with a filled team body and cap, a white box head, two 5 px square eyes, a one-line mouth, no nose and a long heavy brim, about 120 units tall. Hands hold the tool, so draw the arms last.

Paint on a ledge is one shape: a thick band (14-20 px) over the top edge with drips cut into its outline, so the rim wraps them. Roller trails are flat and low-lump. Sprayer landings get drips and one splat. Ramps get a band with no drips.

Jokes are grey, handwritten, few, and kept out of the play space. Each one labels the emptiness as a decision ('sky: done.', 'sun (to scale)', 'bird.', a dimension line reading 120), and none adds a drawn object.
variants.self: Strongest: paint pops harder than in round 1, because the world gives it no competition. The pencil rim makes yellow and green swatches read clearly on white, and at 480x270 both figures, their tools and the blue/orange split are legible. The hatching gives surfaces a value without breaking the no-fill rule, and the grey jokes make the empty sky look like a decision. Weaker: the large hatched floor block is the busiest texture in the frame and could fight the paint on a busy pane, so a sparser hatch on the floor is worth trying. The pencil rims on dense mist specks read slightly gritty and dark up close. The jokes vanish at quarter pane, which is fine since they are outside the play space, but the purist charm is mostly a full-screen thing. The sheet's team-B label uses a darkened orange for legibility, which is a label colour, not a world colour. Each final PNG was rendered from the final SVG.
keep: Paint as the only saturated fill in the world, with team hue kept out of the structure. This is the main reason paint pops harder here than in round 1, and it fits any final style.

A black pencil rim under every wet shape (paint-order stroke, about 2.5 px showing), including drips, droplets and airbrush specks. The character sheet shows yellow and green holding on white because of it. Make this rule universal.
Ledge paint drawn as one keylined band with drips cut into its outline. It reads as one shape at 480x270, unlike round 1's ragged strokes.

The figure spec: 6 px line, filled team shirt and cap, long heavy brim, white box head, two square eyes, no nose. Both figures and their tools read at quarter pane, which fixes round 1's hairline specks.
The sprayer redesign: a white gun body with a team-colour reservoir mounted on top, held at arm's length so it never covers the torso. Large rimmed droplets in the arc.
The roller as a cylinder in three-quarter view with an end ellipse on a long pencil handle, laying a flat, low-lump trail.
Floating platforms with no hang-lines, which cleans up the sky.
A line-weight hierarchy enforced in code (people 6, world 4, notes 3; black for things, grey for notes). It is cheap and makes crude look intentional.
One or two grey handwritten jokes outside the play space ('sky: done.', 'sun (to scale)' as an empty circle). These are good full-screen and capsule flavour, and cost nothing.
drop: The 45-degree hatching as the main ground texture. It reads as an architect's section drawing rather than MS Paint (Paint has no hatch tool), and the big floor block is the busiest thing in the frame at quarter pane. Prefer flat light-grey bucket fill or a much sparser hatch.
Drips hanging down into solid hatched ground on the floor. They read as paint inside the earth. Keep drips to ledge faces and overhangs.

Near-total emptiness as the final direction. The user's favourite is maximalism, and this frame looks clean but sparse, more 'minimalist webcomic' than 'Paint.exe'. Use its rules as the discipline layer under a busier world, not as the whole look.
The dimension-line joke ('120') next to the player. It sits inside the play area and becomes noise at quarter pane.
Pencil rims on dense mist specks, which read gritty and dark. Rim the droplets and the landed paint, and leave the fine mist unrimmed or use a lighter rim.
variants.verdict: Execution is solid and the files are clean. This is the most readable variation of the idea: the paint pops, the figures and tools read at 480x270, and the pencil-rim rule fixes the yellow-on-white failure. As a direction it is the wrong end of the dial for an author whose favourite is maximalism. The frame looks confident but sparse, and the hatching drifts toward technical drawing rather than MS Paint. Its value is as the rulebook for the final combined style: paint is the only saturated fill, every wet shape gets a black rim, ledge paint is one band with drips, the figure spec, the sprayer and roller redesigns, and the line-weight hierarchy. Put those under a fuller, bucket-filled Paint.exe world, and keep the grey jokes as margin flavour.

identity.reason: Very readable and confident, with a useful rulebook. It is the opposite of the maximalism the author picked, though, and the hatching reads as a technical drawing rather than MS Paint.

production.reason: The most readable frame and the cheapest to make, but it is the wrong end of the dial for an author who asked for maximalism. The 45-degree hatching reads as an architectural drawing (Paint has no hatch tool). Its value is as the rulebook discipline layer.

player.reason: Very readable with confident rules, but it is the opposite end of the dial from the maximalism the user likes. The hatching reads as an architectural drawing, not Paint, and its capsule appeal is low. Useful only as the rulebook layer.

variants.brief: NOT a scene. Vary line weight (1x/2x/3x), body (stick limbs vs filled body vs overalls), cap size and brim, head size and eye style, and a silhouette accent such as a cap bobble or brim stripe that could tell same-team players apart. Label each variant with a short Paint-style hand label, A to H. Below or to the side, repeat the same line-up at quarter-pane scale (about 28 px tall) so readability is obvious. character.svg: the best 2–3 variants at large size, in idle, run, jump, hit and painting poses, with sprayer and roller, in all 6 team colours. Keep the original's soul: box head, two dot eyes, flat mouth, flat cap.
variants.one_liner: A figure study: 8 box-head painter variants (A-H) at real 110 px size and again at 28 px quarter-pane size, with silhouette and teammate-accent tests. Three picks (E overalls 2x, F fat-limb big-head 3x, H overalls 3x) are worked up into a pose sheet that also shows all six team slots.
variants.changed: The round-1 painter used a 3-4 px pencil line on a 118 px stick figure and became a hairline speck at quarter pane. This study varies the figure itself instead of drawing a scene. scene.svg compares line weights (1x=3, 2x=6, 3x=9 px), body types (stick, fat limbs, overalls with team-tinted trouser legs), cap size and brim length, head size (up to a chibi head), eye styles (dot, chunky, tall) and neutral accents (brim stripe, bobble, neck flap, antenna). Below that, the same eight figures are built at full scale and the whole row is shrunk to 28 px, so slab, paint and line all scale together as the camera would scale them. That is repeated for blue/orange, pink/green and blue/yellow, plus an all-black silhouette row, a teammates row (same colour, accent only) and a quarter pane in play where round-1 A sits next to H and E. Panel findings addressed: (1) The keyline is now drawn outside the bucket fill using paint-order=stroke. A heavy line can no longer eat the team colour, so a 3x line still leaves a full block of tint. (2) Every paint edge has a black keyline underneath, so yellow reads on grey. (3) The sprayer tank moved off the torso to a back-mounted tank with a team-tinted gauge window, joined by a hose to a pistol-grip lance with a tinted nozzle. (4) The roller is drawn end-on as a tinted wheel and cylinder, because in side view you see the end of the sleeve. It reads as a wheel, not a box, and has a longer handle. (5) Team regions are only cap crown, body or bib, trouser legs, gauge, nozzle and sleeve. Accents are white or black so they survive tinting. character.svg shows E (blue, sprayer), F (orange, roller) and H (yellow, sprayer) in idle, run, jump, hit (X eyes, enemy-colour splat) and painting poses. It also has big weapon callouts and three pair slabs holding all six slots, with overpainted seams. The jokes stay Paint-native: file names in the titles, 'pick one. do NOT add a nose.', the picks circled in pencil, and pose names written on the slabs.
rules: Line weight scales with the figure: at least 6 px pencil on a 110 px painter (2x), so it still lands at about 1.5 px at quarter pane. Never use the round-1 3 px line for characters; keep 3 px for props and UI doodles.

Keyline outside, fill inside: draw the black outline under the bucket fill (paint-order stroke) so the team colour block keeps its full area at any line weight. Drop 1-3 white unfilled specks inside the edge for the leaky-bucket joke.

Team tint goes on big flat blocks only: cap crown, body or overalls bib, trouser legs, sprayer gauge and nozzle, roller sleeve. Head, shirt, eyes, hands, brim and accents stay black or white, so runtime tinting and teammate accents never collide.
Same-team players are told apart by silhouette accents that live above the head: bobble or antenna. Stripes and flaps on the cap are 110 px decoration only and vanish at 28 px.
Every paint edge on a surface gets a 4 px black keyline under it, drips included, so yellow, green and pink read on the grey slab. World structure stays grey, black and white, never a team hue.

Draw weapons as their side-view truth: the sprayer is a back tank plus hose plus lance, never on the belly, and the roller is the end-on wheel of the sleeve on a long brown handle. Keep the tinted part as the largest block of the weapon.
Keep the soul fixed: box head, two square dot eyes (X eyes only on hit), one flat mouth line, flat cap with a straight black brim, no nose. Change proportions, never features.
variants.self: The comparison delivers. In the 28 px rows and the in-play pane, the 1x round-1 figure (A) shrinks to a hairline, while the overalls and fat-limb 2x/3x variants keep a coloured block and a cap shape. The silhouette row shows F and H are the most distinct shapes. The outside keyline was the key technical fix, because heavy lines had been swallowing the team colour on C, F and H. The pose sheet reads as deliberate: the chunky 3x figures have strong poster energy, and the yellow H row holds up thanks to the keylines. The end-on roller and back-tank sprayer read clearly. Weaknesses: the 28 px rows are honest but small and look sparse in the full 1600 frame. At the 480x270 render of the whole sheet the small rows become dots (expected, since that is a quarter pane of a quarter pane). The teammate-accent row honestly shows that only bobble and antenna survive at 28 px, so the accent system needs bigger head-top shapes. Some hit-pose splats float a bit, and the F jump pose's roller arm is awkward. The 3x overalls (H) can get top-heavy and black at the cap; the best balance is probably a hybrid of E's body, F's 3x line and a bobble or antenna. variants.verdict: This is a useful study that solves the style's main weakness, small figures. The lineup shows plainly that round-1 A vanishes at 28 px while E, F and H keep a coloured block and a cap shape, so readability goes up from about 3 to about 6. The outside-keyline fix is the key technical result. With black under every paint edge, all six team colours read, yellow included. The pose sheet looks deliberate and still feels like MS Paint: it is funny, deadpan and cheap to make. The weapon redesigns read clearly. One limit remains: at quarter pane, teammates can still only be told apart by tiny marks on top of the head, so the accent system needs larger shapes.
